Posted May 3, 2001
By Paul Armentano, Special to MarijuanaNews
Paul Armentano is the Senior Policy Analyst for The NORML Foundation, a legal, educational and research organization based in Washington DC.
(MarijuanaNews note: Paul Armentano’s recent return to NORML – with a promotion -- is most welcome. He is an outstanding writer who has an exceptional knowledge of the cannabis issues.)
See
Testimony Of NORML Director of Publications On DEA Ditchweed Eradication Program;
Outstanding Report!

The Supreme Court heard oral arguments for the first time this March regarding whether persons who violate federal marijuana laws may successfully argue the defense of " medical necessity " to avoid criminal prosecution.
See
California Attorney General Supports Medical Marijuana in Oakland CBC Supreme Court Case. Other Medical Marijuana States’ AGs Betray the Sick and Dying.
and links

Throughout the proceedings, Justice Department officials stubbornly argued that marijuana is a prohibited substance with no accepted medical value — a position that implicitly rejects the findings of the highly publicized Institute of Medicine medical marijuana report.

Lawyers for the defendants, the Oakland Buyers’ Cooperative — a non-profit organization that distributed marijuana to patients who possessed a doctor’s recommendation to use it — disagreed. OCBC attorneys cited a July 2000 Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruling that stipulated there exists a class of patients who benefit therapeutically from marijuana and to deny them availability to it runs contrary to the " public interest. " Lawyers argued that this patient protection must also extend to organizations hat supply the ill with their medicine.

The fate of the OCBC and the patients who rely upon its operation now lies in the hands of eight justices (Justice Stephen Breyer recused himself from the case.), who are expected to reach their decision by July. Nevertheless, whichever way our highest court rules, one thing remains certain: Our elected officials’ failure to govern responsibly on this issue has forced voters and the courts to become the ultimate arbiters of our nation’s medical marijuana policy.

It isn’t supposed to be this way. Throughout history, the public has looked to Congress — not the courts — to be the architects of public policy. Yet, despite more than thirty years of mounting scientific evidence and overwhelming public support (Seventy-three percent of Americans now agree that doctor’s should be able to legally prescribe pot, according to a March 21 national Pew Research poll.) in favor of amending the legal status of medical marijuana, federal lawmakers have chosen to hide their collective heads in the sand. Their abdication on this issue has left seriously ill patients with few alternatives: take their issue directly to the voting booth, or take their issue directly to the courts. They have done both.

In 1972, the National Organization for the Reform of Marijuana Laws (NORML) filed an administrative petition with the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) arguing that marijuana met the federal criteria of a prescriptive drug. NORML’s petition called on the federal government to reclassify marijuana as a Schedule II substance, a categorization that would permit physicians to legally prescribe it while maintaining restrictions on its recreational use.

Federal authorities initially refused to accept the petition until mandated to do so by the U.S. Court of Appeals in 1974, and then refused to properly process it until again ordered by the Court in 1982. Legal battles continued until 1986 when the DEA finally allowed rescheduling hearings to take place.

Hearings lasted two years, culminating in 1988 when DEA Administrative Law Judge Francis Young ruled that a sufficient percentage of the medical community recognized the therapeutic uses of marijuana, and that it met the standards of other legal medications. Young recommended: " The Administrator transfer marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule II, to make it available as a legal medicine. It would be unreasonable, arbitrary and capricious for DEA to continue to stand between those sufferers and the benefits of this substance in light of the evidence in this record. "

Nevertheless, then-DEA Administrator John Lawn rejected Young’s determination, choosing instead to impose his own alternative set of rescheduling criteria. Among these, Lawn argued " the substance’s chemistry must be scientifically established to permit it to be reproduced in dosages which can be standardized, " a criteria that a plant medicine such as marijuana would likely never be able to meet.

The DEA further demanded: " The drug must have a New Drug Application (NDA) approved by the Food and Drug Administration, " (One wonders how any drug would placed in Schedule 1, which by definition must have " no currently accepted medical use, " could simultaneously have FDA approval.) or that there must exist " no material
conflict of opinion among experts " as to its safety and effectiveness. Not surprisingly, the DEA found that marijuana failed to meet these new thresholds (Few, if any, substances would.), and the U.S. Court of Appeals in 1994 upheld their decision. As a result, federal law continues to bar doctors from prescribing marijuana to their patients, and seriously ill patients may still be arrested and imprisoned for using it.

Wary of becoming entangled in additional, drawn-out legal challenges, patients and their supporters began taking their issues straight to the voters. Since 1996, nine states — Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Hawaii, Maine, Nevada, Oregon and Washington — have enacted laws exempting patients who use marijuana under their doctor’s supervision from criminal prosecution under state law.

Of these, only Hawaii has done so legislatively; all others have done so via the state initiative process. In response to this trend, federal officials funded a million dollar, 18-month investigation by the National Academy of Sciences to determine marijuana’s medical utility. In 1999, investigators concluded: " Scientific data indicate the potential therapeutic value of cannabinoid drugs, primarily THC, for pain relief, control of nausea and vomiting, and appetite stimulation. Except for the harms associated with smoking, the adverse effects of marijuana use are within the range tolerated for other medications. "

They further added that inhaling cannabis " would be advantageous " in the treatment of some diseases, and that the herb’s short-term medical benefits outweigh any smoking related harms for some patients. The release of the report came just months after a United Kingdom Parliamentary inquiry issued similar conclusions, and affirmed " this evidence is enough to justify a change in the law. " (Parliament summarily rejected the commission’s findings the same day they were released.)

Although the unveiling of these prestigious and highly publicized reports offered U.S. lawmakers the ideal opportunity to re-assess federal law in a scientific, non-partisan manner, they once again failed to act. In fact, the only recent vote Congress has taken on the issue was a 1998 sense of the House resolution defining marijuana as a " dangerous " substance that " should not be legalized for medical use. " Lawmakers perpetual intransigence makes it apparent that they are out of touch with both the scientific evidence and the views of their constituents on this issue.

Judicial activism rarely makes for sound public policy. In this case, however, Congress has given the justices no alternative. By refusing to enact rational federal reforms when given the opportunity, they have forced voters, and now the high court to determine our federal policy on medical marijuana. Let’s hope they do so with more common sense and compassion than their Washington colleagues.
